# Problem 1

### Create a birthday function
Write a function that, for a fixed group size, randomly draws “birthdays” for each person
```{r}
birthday_check = function(n) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)

  n_distinct(birthdays) < n
}
```

### Test the function
duplicate birthdays in the group; and returns TRUE or FALSE based on the result.
```{r}
set.seed(1)
birthday_check(7)
birthday_check(77)
birthday_check(245)
```

### Run the simulations
Next, run this function 10000 times for each group size between 2 and 50.
```{r}
set.seed(1)

birthday_results = 
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |> 
  mutate(shared_birthday = map_lgl(group_size, birthday_check))
```


### Calculate the probabilities
compute the probability that at least two people in the group will share a birthday by averaging across the 10000 simulation runs.
```{r}
birthday_summary = 
  birthday_results |> 
  group_by(group_size) |> 
  summarize(probability = mean(shared_birthday))
birthday_summary
```

### Plot the results
Make a plot showing the probability as a function of group size, and comment on your results.
```{r}
birthday_summary |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point() + 
  labs(
    title = "Probability of sharing a birthday by group size",
    x = "Group size",
    y = "Probability of at least one shared birthday"
  )
```

The chance of a shared birthday increases pretty quickly as the group gets bigger. It first passes 50% at a group size of `r birthday_summary |> filter(probability > 0.5) |> pull(group_size) |> min()`. By the time there are 50 people, the probability reaches `r round(birthday_summary |> filter(group_size == 50) |> pull(probability), 2)`. This is surprising because even a small group can have many possible pairs of people, making a shared birthday more likely.

## Problem 2

### Import the data

I used list.files() to get the file names and map() to read the data for each subject.
```{r}
full_df = 
  tibble(
    files = list.files("data/"),
    path = str_c("data/", files)
  ) |> 
  mutate(data = map(path, read_csv)) |> 
  unnest()
```

### Tidy the data
I tidy the result and manipulate file names to include control arm and subject ID, make sure weekly observations are “tidy”.
```{r}
tidy_df = 
  full_df |> 
  mutate(
    files = str_replace(files, ".csv", ""),
    group = str_sub(files, 1, 3)) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "outcome",
    names_prefix = "week_") |> 
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |> 
  select(group, subj = files, week, outcome)
```

### Spaghetti plot
I make a spaghetti plot showing observations on each subject over time.
```{r}
tidy_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = outcome, group = subj, color = group)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_path() + 
  facet_grid(~group) + 
  labs(
    title = "Observations over time by subject",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Outcome",
    color = "Arm"
  )
```

The control group shows little change over time, while the experimental group generally shows an increasing trend. 
There are also differences between individual subjects within each group.

## Problem 3

### Create a simulation function
First, I created a function to simulates a dataset.
```{r}
sim_t_test = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {
  sim_data = tibble(
    x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  )
  t.test(pull(sim_data, x), mu = 0) |> 
    broom::tidy() |> 
    select(estimate, p.value)
}
```

### Test the function
```{r}
sim_t_test(mu = 0)
sim_t_test(mu = 4)
```
### Run the simulations
I generated 5000 datasets for each true mean from 0 to 6
```{r}
sim_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |> 
  mutate(estimate_df = map(mu, sim_t_test)) |> 
  unnest(estimate_df)
```

### Calculate power
I calculated power as the proportion of tests with a p-value below 0.05 for each true mean.
```{r}
power_df = 
  sim_results_df |> 
  group_by(mu) |> 
  summarize(power = mean(p.value < 0.05))
power_df 
```

### Plot power
```{r}
power_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = power)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point() + 
  labs(
    title = "Power of a one-sample t-test by true mean",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Proportion of times the null was rejected"
  )
```

As the true mean increases, the power also increases. 
This is because a larger effect size makes it easier to reject the null hypothesis.
When mu = 0, the rejection rate is around 5%, while for larger values of mu, the power approaches 1.

### Average estimates from all samples
```{r}
all_results =
  sim_results_df |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(mean_estimate = mean(estimate)) |>
  mutate(group = "All samples")
all_results
```

### Average estimates from rejected tests
```{r}
rejected_results =
  sim_results_df |>
  filter(p.value < 0.05) |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(mean_estimate = mean(estimate)) |>
  mutate(group = "Null rejected")
rejected_results
```
The average estimates from all samples are generally close to the true values of mu.

### Plot the average estimates
```{r}
bind_rows(all_results, rejected_results) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = mean_estimate, color = group)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated Mean by True Mean",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Average estimated mean",
    color = "Samples"
  )
```

The average estimates from rejected tests are not always close to the true values, especially when the true mean is small. 
That makes sense because samples that happen to show larger effects are more likely to reject the null hypothesis. 
When the true mean is large, nearly all tests reject the null, so the average estimates are close to the true values.
